topics.title: What venture capital is
topics.technical: VC funds high-risk, high-growth startups in exchange for equity, betting a fund on a few outsized winners paying for many losses. It is an asset class with its own power-law logic, distinct from ordinary investing.
topics.simple: Investing in risky young startups, expecting a few huge wins to cover many failures.

topics.title: The startup funding lifecycle
topics.technical: From pre-seed and seed through Series A, B and beyond to exit, each stage funds a different risk: idea, product, growth, scale. Knowing the ladder frames every valuation and expectation.
topics.simple: The stages of raising money — each buying down a different startup risk.

topics.title: How VC funds work
topics.technical: A fund pools limited partners' capital, deploys it over years, and returns gains after fees and carry. The 2-and-20 structure and the ten-year clock shape every incentive in the business.
topics.simple: How the money is pooled, invested, and shared between investors and fund managers.

topics.title: Sourcing deals
topics.technical: Deal flow comes from networks, referrals, accelerators and outreach; seeing many companies is prerequisite to picking well. Proprietary flow is a real edge — the best deals are often not advertised.
topics.simple: Finding promising startups to invest in — the more you see, the better you choose.

topics.title: Evaluating founders and teams
topics.technical: Early-stage bets are bets on people: coachability, resilience, insight and complementary teams predict more than the plan, which will change. VCs back founders who navigate uncertainty, not just present well.
topics.simple: Judging the people, because at the start the team matters more than the plan.

topics.title: Market sizing and opportunity
topics.technical: VCs need markets big enough for outsized returns: TAM/SAM/SOM, growth rate and timing separate a lifestyle business from a venture-scale one. A great team in a tiny market still cannot return a fund.
topics.simple: Checking the opportunity is huge enough for a startup to become enormous.

topics.title: Business models and unit economics
topics.technical: CAC, LTV, margins and payback reveal whether growth creates or destroys value; a model that loses more per customer as it scales is a trap. Unit economics is where hype meets arithmetic.
topics.simple: Does the company make money per customer, or lose more the bigger it gets?

topics.title: Reading pitch decks
topics.technical: A deck signals clarity of thought: problem, solution, market, traction, team, ask. VCs read for substance and honesty behind the polish, and for what is conspicuously missing.
topics.simple: What investors actually look for behind a startup's pitch slides.

topics.title: Traction and metrics
topics.technical: Growth, retention, engagement and revenue quality show whether a product works; vanity metrics flatter while cohort and retention data tell the truth. Traction de-risks the bet more than any story.
topics.simple: The real numbers that prove a startup is working, not just talking.

topics.title: Valuation basics
topics.technical: Early-stage valuation blends comparables, ownership targets and negotiation more than DCF; pre- and post-money math determines who owns what. Price is a negotiated bet on the future, not a calculated fact.
topics.simple: How startups get a price tag before profits — mostly negotiation and comparison.

topics.title: Term sheets
topics.technical: Term sheets set valuation, liquidation preferences, board seats, option pools and protective provisions — control and economics both. The headline number matters less than the terms beneath it.
topics.simple: The deal's real terms — who controls what and who gets paid first.

topics.title: Cap tables and dilution
topics.technical: A cap table tracks ownership across rounds; each raise dilutes existing holders, and option pools and preferences reshape who actually profits at exit. Founders and investors alike live or die by this math.
topics.simple: Who owns how much — and how each new investment shrinks everyone's slice.

topics.title: Due diligence
topics.technical: Before investing, VCs verify the team, market, tech, financials and legals; diligence catches the gap between pitch and reality. Skipping it is how avoidable disasters get funded.
topics.simple: Checking a startup's claims are true before writing the cheque.

topics.title: Portfolio strategy
topics.technical: VCs build portfolios expecting most to fail and few to return the fund; diversification, reserves for follow-on, and ownership targets manage the power law. One winner can pay for everything.
topics.simple: Spreading bets knowing most lose, because one giant win covers all.

topics.title: Supporting portfolio companies
topics.technical: Beyond capital, VCs help with hiring, introductions, strategy and follow-on funding; the best add real value between rounds. Money is a commodity; help is the differentiator.
topics.simple: What good investors do after investing — hiring, intros, advice, more money.

topics.title: Exits: IPOs and acquisitions
topics.technical: Returns come only at exit — acquisition or IPO — so VCs think about the buyer from the start. Timing, market conditions and preferences decide who profits and how much.
topics.simple: How investors finally cash out — being bought or going public.

topics.title: Risk and failure
topics.technical: Most startups fail; VCs manage risk through portfolio construction, staged funding and honest post-mortems, not by avoiding failure. Understanding failure modes improves the next bet.
topics.simple: Failure is normal — good investors plan for it and learn from it.

topics.title: The founder's perspective
topics.technical: Understanding fundraising from the founder's side — dilution fear, control, the fundraising grind — makes for better, more aligned investors. The relationship is a long marriage, not a transaction.
topics.simple: Seeing the deal through the founder's eyes makes for a better partner.

topics.title: Emerging trends
topics.technical: Sectors, geographies and models shift; AI, climate and new fund structures reshape where capital flows. Reading trends early is part of the edge, though hype must be discounted.
topics.simple: Spotting where the next wave of startups and money is heading.

topics.title: Ethics and the ecosystem
topics.technical: VC shapes which futures get built and funded; access, bias and incentive misalignment are real problems the industry wrestles with. Capital allocation is a form of power with consequences.
topics.simple: The responsibility that comes with deciding which ideas get funded.

topics.title: The capstone
topics.technical: Evaluate a real startup as an investor: market, team, model, traction, valuation and a reasoned invest/pass memo with terms. An investment memo demonstrates the whole analytical discipline.
topics.simple: Write a full invest-or-pass analysis of a real startup — the VC's core deliverable.
